prompt.context: Your client is the owner of UPS #88, a racecar on the NASCAR tour. It races in the Nextel Cup, a points-based championship where the season winner has accumulated the most points over the course of the racing season. There are 36 races in total, running from February to November. Dale Jarrett, a well-known celebrity driver, races for the team. Dale helped win the Nextel Cup three years ago, and so far this year is eighth in a field of 43 drivers. A close friend who is the VP of marketing at Home Depot recently contacted the client. She inquired about sponsoring a second racing team with the client. She recognizes that NASCAR is the fastest growing segment among males ages 18-45. She also has talked to a successful driver from a regional drag racing circuit to try out as the driver of the team.
prompt.question: Evaluate the potential of this opportunity. Specifically, should the client add a second racing team sponsored by Home Depot?

clarifying_info.q: What revenue sources does the team currently have?
clarifying_info.a: Interviewer provides Exhibit 1 (after candidate brainstorms revenue buckets first).

clarifying_info.q: What are the team's current costs?
clarifying_info.a: Interviewer provides Exhibit 2 (after candidate brainstorms cost buckets first). Total costs are $20M.

clarifying_info.q: How many races does the new driver qualify for?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the driver qualifies for 30 of 36 races.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average race winnings per race?
clarifying_info.a: Race winnings range from $50K to $1M per race; assume an average of $200K (other reasonable assumptions are acceptable).

clarifying_info.q: Which costs increase if a second team is added?
clarifying_info.a: Race-facing salaries, equipment, and travel costs will each double. Engine shop and R&D costs (Lease and R&D lines) are shared and do not change.

exhibits.title: Revenue Sources
exhibits.shows: A table listing the four revenue sources for the current NASCAR team, each with a percentage of total revenues and a short description.

data.Sponsorships: 60% of revenues — UPS dominates; other sponsors include Outback Steakhouse and 3M
data.Nextel Cup Race Winnings: 25% of revenues — winnings range from $50K to $1M per race depending on finish and race significance
data.Selling Engines: 10% of revenues — strong R&D shop; engines sold to professional drivers domestically
data.Merchandising: 5% of revenues — licensed to third-party; T-shirts and caps

exhibits.title: Cost Breakdown
exhibits.shows: A table listing the five cost categories for the current team, each with a percentage of total costs and a short description.

data.Salary: 40% of costs — race-facing (mechanics and Dale Jarrett) = 50% of salary line; non-race-facing (engine shop technicians, HR, accounting) = 50% of salary line
data.Equipment: 25% of costs — race cars, engines, parts (sheet metal)
data.Travel: 5% of costs — getting to and from races
data.Lease, engine shop: 10% of costs — leasing of land in rural North Carolina
data.R&D: 20% of costs — engine shop technology improvements

framework: Profitability of existing team: establish baseline revenue and cost structure
Revenue build-up for new team: use race winnings % share to extrapolate total revenue
Cost analysis for new team: identify which cost buckets are incremental vs. shared
Minimum sponsorship ask from Home Depot: incremental costs set the floor
Market entry attractiveness: growth of NASCAR fan base, Home Depot brand fit, competitive alternatives
Risks and qualifications: new driver profile, resource dilution, assumption sensitivity

questions.prompt: What is the current team's total annual revenue?
questions.guidance: Candidate should first brainstorm revenue buckets (sponsorships, race winnings, engine sales, merchandise) then receive Exhibit 1. The only quantifiable data given is race winnings. Candidate must estimate total winnings and back-calculate total revenue using the 25% share. Key steps: (1) estimate average winnings, (2) multiply by races qualified, (3) divide by 0.25.

math.setup: Race winnings = avg winnings per race × races qualified; Total revenue = Race winnings / (race winnings % of total)
steps: Average race winnings = $200K (range $50K–$1M; $200K is a reasonable midpoint)
Race winnings are 25% of total revenue → Total revenue = $6M / 0.25 = $24M

questions.prompt: What is the current team's profit?
questions.guidance: Interviewer tells candidate that total costs are $20M. Candidate should compute simple profit after arriving at the $24M revenue figure.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum amount the client should charge Home Depot for sponsorship (i.e., what are the marginal costs of adding the second team)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify which cost lines are incremental. Race-facing salaries, equipment, and travel double; lease and R&D are shared (engine shop is already built). Marginal cost = incremental amounts from those three lines applied to the $20M base.

math.setup: Marginal cost = incremental salary (race-facing only) + incremental equipment + incremental travel
steps: Race-facing salary = 50% of 40% of $20M = 0.50 × 0.40 × $20M = $4M; doubles → incremental = $4M
math.answer: Minimum sponsorship ask = $10M (marginal cost of new team)

questions.prompt: Should the client charge a premium above the $10M marginal cost to Home Depot?
questions.guidance: No single right answer; interviewer evaluates quality of reasoning. Strong candidates present both sides and reach a defended conclusion. Option 1 (Yes — charge a premium): Home Depot has already begun negotiations with a driver, signaling commitment and giving client bargaining power; premium can be justified via ROI analysis showing brand reach to males 18-45, the fastest-growing NASCAR demographic. Option 2 (No — do not charge a premium): Home Depot has alternatives — another race team, another sport (e.g., baseball), or another racing circuit (e.g., Formula One); excessive premium may lose the deal.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key risks of adding this second NASCAR team?

categories.name: Driver quality and profile
ideas: New driver has only drag racing experience — skill transferability to oval/road courses is unproven
Driver lacks name recognition, likely reducing merchandising revenue contribution
Celebrity endorsement and fan base of Dale Jarrett cannot be replicated by an unknown driver

categories.name: Resource dilution
ideas: High-quality mechanics from Dale's team may be redirected to the new team, diluting performance of the flagship car
Management bandwidth split across two teams could hurt operational quality
Engine shop capacity may become a constraint if both teams compete for R&D resources

categories.name: Cost assumptions
ideas: Salary for new team may be lower than assumed because the driver lacks Dale Jarrett's star power
Equipment costs may be lower than average due to shared engine shop technology — some leverage already exists
Closing the engine shop could reduce costs, but margin information is unavailable to substantiate this

categories.name: Sponsorship and revenue risk
ideas: Home Depot may withdraw if deal economics are unfavorable; concentration risk if one sponsor funds the entire new team
Race winnings for an unproven driver are likely below $200K average — revenue may be overstated
Merchandising revenue from new team near zero given driver's anonymity

categories.name: Competitive/market risk
ideas: NASCAR is growing, but Home Depot has competing sponsorship options across sports and racing circuits
If the new team performs poorly, reputational spillover could harm the flagship UPS #88 brand

categories.name: Operational/logistical risk
ideas: Coordinating two teams across 36 races (30 qualifying) significantly increases travel and scheduling complexity
Regulatory or NASCAR rules changes could affect the economics of fielding multiple teams

recommendation: The opportunity is financially viable: with $10M in incremental costs and the potential to fully offset them through Home Depot's sponsorship, the marginal team could break even or generate incremental profit if sponsorship is priced above cost

Recommend proceeding with the second team, contingent on Home Depot committing to a sponsorship of at least $10M (the marginal cost floor), with a premium justified by the demographic reach of NASCAR's 18-45 male audience
risks: New driver's lack of NASCAR experience could result in below-average race winnings and near-zero merchandising revenue, making the $200K average winnings assumption overly optimistic
Resource dilution — especially high-quality mechanics — could hurt Dale Jarrett's existing team performance, threatening the flagship Nextel Cup standing
Home Depot retains alternatives (other teams, other sports, Formula One) that limit pricing leverage
next_steps: Negotiate sponsorship fee with Home Depot at or above $10M; conduct ROI analysis to justify premium pricing
Assess the drag racing driver's potential for oval/road course NASCAR performance; consider a development or test period
Model downside scenario with lower average race winnings (e.g., $100K) to stress-test profitability before committing
Clarify engine shop sharing rules and mechanic allocation to prevent dilution of the flagship team
